strengths: The paper targets an important and timely gap: evaluation of long-form, complex text-to-video generation, where short-video benchmarks and simple prompts are clearly insufficient.

LoCoT2V-Bench is reasonably broad in design, with 240 real-video-derived prompts across 18 themes, long prompts averaging about 237 words, and evaluation of nine representative open-source long-video generation methods.

The benchmark covers useful dimensions beyond standard visual quality, including event-level alignment, transition smoothness, intra/inter-event consistency, content clarity, and high-level human-expectation dimensions such as narrative flow and thematic expression.

The paper provides substantial implementation detail in the appendix, including prompt templates, metric formulas, baseline descriptions, theme/category analyses, and numerical breakdowns across many subdimensions.

The empirical results are informative: they show that current methods often score well on static quality and short-term consistency but struggle with event-level alignment, transition smoothness, inter-event consistency, narrative flow, and character development.
weaknesses: The central weakness is insufficient validation of the proposed metrics. Many important scores rely on MLLMs/LLMs, semantic similarity, generated descriptions, or yes/no VQA, but the paper does not show convincing correlation with human judgments, inter-rater agreement, metric reliability, or sensitivity/specificity analyses.

HERD and content-clarity claims are especially under-supported. The benchmark uses MLLMs to generate high-level expectations from source videos, generate questions, annotate polarity, and evaluate generated videos, creating a heavily model-mediated pipeline whose biases and failure modes are not empirically validated.

Reproducibility is weak for a benchmark paper. The reproducibility statement says code and full release will come later, and the URL appears blank. Several components depend on specific large models and tools, including Qwen2.5-VL, DeepSeek-V3.1, Seed1.5-VL, Time-R1, Grounded-SAM-2, RAFT, and proprietary or rapidly changing systems, but exact settings, versions, prompts for all stages, seeds, and generated artifacts are not sufficiently packaged for reuse.

The dataset scale is modest for the breadth of claims: 240 prompts across 18 themes is useful, but small relative to the diversity of long-form video generation. The paper does not provide enough evidence that the selected YouTube-derived videos and manual filtering yield representative coverage.

The evaluation design may conflate prompt adherence with evaluator/model assumptions. For example, event extraction, event matching, and video description are all mediated by LLM/VLM outputs, so errors in understanding generated videos can directly affect alignment and consistency scores.

The paper lacks adequate human baselines or sanity checks. It would be important to compare metric rankings against human pairwise preferences or expert ratings, include adversarial or controlled videos with known failures, and report variance across repeated MLLM evaluations.

Some metric normalizations and aggregations appear ad hoc. Averaging many heterogeneous submetrics into five dimensions and then an overall score may obscure reliability differences and produce rankings whose practical meaning is unclear.

The ethical statement is too shallow. It asserts compliance with YouTube terms and copyright regulations despite collecting videos via yt-dlp, but does not discuss licensing, consent, redistribution of prompts derived from videos, creator rights, or possible benchmark leakage from public videos.

Presentation is generally understandable but uneven. There are typos, grammar issues, and some confusing notation, including overloaded abbreviations such as TQ for both technical quality and temporal quality, and several claims of robustness are stronger than the evidence supports.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: evaluation of long-form, complex text-to-video generation, where existing short-clip benchmarks are indeed insufficient.

The benchmark attempts broad coverage, with 240 prompts across 18 themes, nine evaluated long-video generation methods, and a multi-dimensional metric suite covering static quality, alignment, temporal quality, content clarity, and higher-level narrative expectations.

Some proposed directions are useful, especially event-level alignment and separating intra-event from inter-event temporal consistency, since long videos often fail through ordering, transition, and cross-shot consistency errors that aggregate metrics hide.

The manuscript includes implementation details and prompt templates in the appendix, and reports several diagnostic analyses such as correlations with static quality, prompt complexity, and content categories.
weaknesses: The central evaluation methodology is not convincingly validated. Many key scores rely on MLLMs/LLMs as judges, captioners, event extractors, prompt complexity scorers, polarity annotators, and question generators, but the paper provides no human correlation study, inter-rater agreement, calibration analysis, or error analysis showing that these automated judgments are reliable for long generated videos.

There is substantial circularity and construct-validity concern in the benchmark design. Prompts and HERD targets are derived from real-world videos using MLLMs, then generated videos are evaluated by related MLLM-based descriptions/questions against those derived targets. This may measure agreement with machine-generated descriptions and subjective expectations rather than robust human-perceived video quality or prompt adherence.

The proposed HERD metric is especially under-supported. Abstract dimensions such as emotional response, interpretive depth, character development, and overall impression are reduced to automatically generated yes/no questions and MLLM answers, with unclear handling of invalid/unclear responses and no evidence that the resulting percentages correspond to human expectation realization.

Several metric definitions are underspecified or questionable. For event-level alignment, the exact embedding model, similarity normalization, matching behavior when events are missing, and score calibration are unclear. Transition smoothness uses an ad hoc weighted combination and variance formula, but weights, window size, scaling constants, and robustness to hard cuts versus intended cinematic cuts are not adequately justified.

The experimental analysis mostly reports benchmark scores without external validation. There is no comparison against human rankings, no ablation isolating new metrics, no sensitivity analysis over LLM choices or prompts, and no uncertainty estimates/statistical tests despite many automated stochastic components.

Originality is moderate rather than strong. The work primarily aggregates existing video quality metrics and LLM/VLM judging pipelines into a new benchmark. The long-form focus is useful, but the methodological novelty is limited and not backed by enough validation to establish the benchmark as reliable.

Reproducibility is weak. The reproducibility statement says prompt data, evaluation code, and results will be released later after reorganization, and even appears to omit the actual release URL. The benchmark depends on many external models/tools, including large proprietary or rapidly changing LLMs/VLMs, YouTube videos, and multiple segmentation/grounding/quality models, making exact reproduction difficult without a concrete artifact release and versioned data.

The ethics statement is too cursory for a benchmark built from YouTube videos. It asserts compliance with terms and copyright but does not specify licensing, redistribution rights, consent, dataset takedown procedures, privacy filtering details, or whether generated prompts/descriptions can leak identifiable information from source videos.

Presentation quality is below the standard expected for a main-track paper. There are frequent grammar errors, formatting problems, cramped tables, inconsistent terminology, and typos such as “adpot,” “perspectively,” and malformed prompt text. These issues make the contribution harder to assess and reduce confidence in execution quality.

The paper’s claims are stronger than the evidence supports. Statements that the benchmark is comprehensive, reliable, robust, and a foundation for rigorous evaluation are not established without human validation, metric reliability analysis, and released reproducible artifacts.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely gap: evaluation of long-form, complex text-to-video generation rather than short, single-scene clips. The benchmark is clearly motivated by current LVG failure modes such as event ordering, long-range consistency, narrative flow, and high-level thematic adherence.

The benchmark design is more ambitious than many prior suites: 240 real-video-derived prompts across 18 themes, substantially longer prompts, five major evaluation dimensions, and 26 subdimensions. The event-level alignment, transition smoothness, content clarity, and HERD dimensions are useful attempts to move beyond frame quality and coarse CLIP-style alignment.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad, covering nine open-source LVG methods and reporting both aggregate and subdimension results. The analysis sections on static-quality bias, prompt complexity, content type effects, and event-alignment/temporal-consistency entanglement make the benchmark more informative than a simple leaderboard.

Presentation is generally clear, with helpful tables, appendices, prompt templates, metric formulas, case studies, and implementation details. The paper is easy to follow despite the breadth of the evaluation framework.
The ethical statement and LLM-usage disclosure are present, and the authors explicitly discuss filtering harmful or inappropriate content and avoiding PII in prompt construction.
weaknesses: The main weakness is limited validation of the proposed automatic metrics against human judgment. HERD and content clarity are explicitly intended to capture human expectations, narrative quality, emotional response, and interpretive depth, but the paper does not provide a human study, inter-rater agreement, or human-correlation analysis demonstrating that the MLLM-based scores are reliable proxies for those constructs.

Several central components depend heavily on proprietary or rapidly changing LLM/MLLM systems, including DeepSeek-V3.1, Qwen2.5-VL-72B, Seed1.5-VL, and other VLM-based evaluators. This raises reproducibility and stability concerns, especially for a benchmark meant to support future comparisons.

The reproducibility statement is incomplete: the paper says prompt data, evaluation code, and benchmark results will be released later, but no usable link is provided in the manuscript text, and the full release is deferred until after code reorganization. For a benchmark paper, this is a material weakness.

The dataset scale is useful but still modest for the breadth of claims: 240 prompts over 18 themes may not be enough to robustly characterize long-form generation across domains, styles, and narrative structures. The paper would benefit from stronger sampling justification and clearer train/test leakage considerations with respect to web/video data.

The construction process starts from YouTube videos and MLLM-generated descriptions. The paper states compliance with terms and copyright regulations, but it is unclear whether source videos can be redistributed, whether generated prompts may preserve copyrighted narrative/cinematic content, and how future users can audit or reproduce the real-video-derived annotations.

Some metrics appear potentially fragile or underspecified in edge cases. For example, event extraction and matching rely on generated video descriptions, event grounding, segmentation, and semantic similarity; failures in any upstream model can affect scores in ways that may be hard to disentangle from generation quality.

The paper would be stronger with ablations over metric choices, evaluator models, number of MLLM trials, prompt-generation variants, and normalization choices. Without these, it is difficult to know whether model rankings are robust to reasonable implementation changes.

Originality is moderate rather than exceptional: the paper extends the benchmark tradition with longer and more complex prompts plus new high-level dimensions, but many building blocks are inherited from VBench, EvalCrafter, MLLM-as-judge pipelines, and existing video quality tools. The contribution is valuable, but not a major methodological breakthrough.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely gap: evaluating long-form, multi-scene text-to-video generation under substantially more complex prompts than most existing benchmarks.

LoCoT2V-Bench is reasonably scoped and useful in principle, with 234 real-video-derived prompts across 18 themes, hierarchical scene/character/background/camera metadata, and longer prompts than prior benchmarks.

The evaluation suite is broad, covering perceptual quality, coarse and fine-grained text-video alignment, temporal quality, dynamic quality, and higher-level expectation realization. The fine-grained gated VQA design is a sensible attempt to diagnose failures beyond global CLIP-style scores.

The empirical section evaluates 13 representative long-video generation methods and reports informative trends, especially the gap between global quality/background consistency and weak fine-grained alignment/character consistency.
The appendix provides many implementation prompts and additional tables, and the authors make some effort to validate automatic metrics against human annotations and compare HERD variants.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is a major concern. Several core components rely on closed or insufficiently specified models such as GPT-5 and a generic strong MLLM, and key parameter choices for sampling, VQA, scoring normalization, metric aggregation, and model prompts are not enough to reproduce the exact benchmark reliably.

The validation of the automatic metrics is not strong enough for the central claims. Human alignment is measured on only 5% of generated videos with three annotators, no reported inter-annotator agreement, no confidence intervals, and only moderate correlations for many dimensions; character consistency, HERD subdimensions, and background consistency have relatively weak human alignment.

The scoring framework combines heterogeneous metrics with mostly uniform or lightly justified averaging. The dynamic-quality aggregate is fit on only 100 annotated videos, and the main average score across PQ/TVA/TQ/HERD/DQ is not clearly justified as a meaningful overall quality measure.

Benchmark construction may introduce bias and ambiguity. Prompts are expanded from real videos using LLMs into story-like descriptions with named characters and inferred narrative details; the paper does not convincingly show that the resulting metadata is complete, objective, or faithful enough to support fine-grained automated evaluation.

Baseline fairness is imperfect. Some models use decomposed multi-prompt inputs while others receive direct prompts, some use official/default resolutions rather than the standardized 480p setting, and StoryAdapter is combined with an external image-to-video model, making comparisons harder to interpret.

The ethics and data discussion is too superficial for a YouTube-derived benchmark. The paper asserts compliance with terms and copyright regulations but does not explain licensing, redistribution rights, creator consent, privacy handling for people appearing in videos, or whether only prompts/metadata rather than videos will be released.

Presentation is generally understandable but has numerous typos, formatting issues, and ambiguities in formulas and tables. Some important details are deferred or vague, including the exact MLLM/VQA models used, HERD evaluator behavior, prompt filtering protocol, and statistical uncertainty of results.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely evaluation gap: long-form, multi-scene text-to-video generation under complex prompts is under-covered by existing short-video benchmarks.

LoCoT2V-Bench has some useful design choices, especially hierarchical metadata for scenes, characters, backgrounds, and camera movement, which could support more diagnostic evaluation than a single global prompt-adherence score.

The paper evaluates a reasonably broad set of 13 long-video generation methods and reports multiple dimensions, revealing plausible weaknesses of current systems in fine-grained text-video alignment and character consistency.
The appendix includes many of the prompts used for LLM-based construction and evaluation, plus additional category-level and sub-dimension results, which helps clarify the intended pipeline.
weaknesses: The core evaluation methodology is not sufficiently sound. Several major metrics rely on opaque LLM/MLLM judgments, including overall alignment, fine-grained VQA, complexity scoring, prompt expansion, prompt verification, and HERD, but the manuscript often describes the judge only as a strong MLLM and does not provide enough information to assess bias, calibration, failure modes, or reproducibility.

Human validation is too weak for the paper's central claims. Only 5% of generated videos are annotated by three annotators, inter-annotator agreement is not reported, and several correlations are only moderate or weak, e.g. fine-grained alignment around SRCC 52.70, character consistency around SRCC 49.90, and HERD sub-dimensions often in the 40s. This does not convincingly establish that LoCoT2V-Eval aligns well with human judgment.

The benchmark construction raises serious validity concerns. Prompts are derived from YouTube videos via MLLM description and then expanded by GPT-5 into story-like prompts, so the benchmark may measure conformance to synthetic, LLM-inflated narratives rather than realistic user intent. The claimed prompt complexity is itself judged by an LLM, which risks circularly rewarding length and verbosity.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The paper depends on closed or fast-moving systems such as GPT-5, DeepSeek-V3.2, Seed1.5-VL, SAM3, and an unspecified strong MLLM, but omits key model versions, decoding parameters, API settings, full metadata release commitments, and implementation details needed to reproduce the scores.

Baseline comparisons are not fully controlled. Some methods are run at default or officially recommended settings rather than the nominal standardized 480p setting, and StoryAdapter is converted into a video method using Wan2.2. These choices may materially affect rankings, but the paper does not analyze their impact.

The scoring aggregation is under-justified. Averaging heterogeneous dimensions into a final score and fitting the dynamic-quality aggregation on only 100 annotated videos are not well motivated, and uncertainty estimates or statistical significance tests are absent.

The paper's originality is limited. Much of LoCoT2V-Eval is a composition of existing IQA, CLIP/feature similarity, VQA, optical-flow, and LLM-as-judge components. HERD is presented as novel, but its formulation is essentially LLM-generated expectations plus LLM-based scoring, with limited evidence that it robustly captures higher-level human expectations.

The ethics and limitations discussion is insufficient. The impact statement asserts compliance with YouTube terms and copyright regulations, but the paper gives no concrete licensing, redistribution, consent, or takedown procedure. It also does not seriously discuss privacy risks, cultural bias in LLM-generated prompts and judges, or benchmark leakage into future video models.

Presentation is polished at a high level but leaves many important technical choices ambiguous. The result tables are extensive, yet the paper does not provide enough diagnostic analysis of when the proposed metrics fail, how sensitive rankings are to judge choice, or whether the same conclusions hold under alternative human-centered evaluation protocols.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely gap: evaluation of long-form, multi-scene text-to-video generation under complex prompts, where existing short-video benchmarks are clearly insufficient.

LoCoT2V-Bench is useful in scope and structure: 234 curated real-world-video-derived prompts across 18 themes, with long prompts, multi-scene structure, character/background/camera metadata, and statistics showing substantially higher prompt length and complexity than several prior benchmarks.

The evaluation suite is thoughtfully multi-dimensional, covering perceptual quality, coarse and fine-grained text-video alignment, temporal quality, dynamic quality, and the proposed HERD dimension for higher-level narrative/viewer-expectation properties.

The experiments are broad for a benchmark paper, evaluating 13 representative long-video generation systems and exposing informative failure modes, especially weak fine-grained alignment and character consistency despite high background consistency and perceptual quality.

The paper includes useful implementation details in the appendix, including prompt templates, baseline settings, dynamic-quality formulas, HERD prompts, category-level results, and case studies, which improves transparency.
The human-alignment study is a meaningful validation effort: automatic scores are compared against three annotators, and several dimensions show moderate to strong correlations with human judgment.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is a concern because several central components rely on powerful proprietary or time-sensitive models/tools, including GPT-5, strong unspecified MLLMs, SAM3, FG-CLIP2, and model-specific generation settings. The manuscript does not clearly state a release plan for data, code, generated videos, annotations, or exact model/API versions.

The human validation is somewhat thin relative to the ambition of the benchmark: only 5% of generated videos are annotated, there is no reported inter-annotator agreement, and several important correlations are only moderate, e.g. character consistency, HERD subdimensions, and dynamic quality. This weakens claims that the full LoCoT2V-Eval suite reliably aligns with human judgment.

Some metric choices may be insufficiently justified. For example, background consistency remains extremely high for nearly all methods, suggesting possible saturation; character consistency depends on successful detection/tracking/verification; and the linear aggregation for dynamic quality is fitted on only 100 annotated videos.

The benchmark prompts are generated and expanded from real videos using MLLMs/LLMs rather than collected from actual user tasks. This gives structure and controllability, but it may introduce stylistic artifacts and model-specific biases, especially since prompt complexity is also judged by an LLM.

The comparison between direct-input and multi-prompt methods is not fully clean: multi-prompt systems receive scene-level decompositions produced with LLM assistance and manual correction, while other systems consume the full prompt directly. This is practical but can confound model capability with prompt preprocessing quality.

The contribution is more integrative than methodologically novel: many submetrics are adapted from prior benchmarks or existing tools. The originality lies mainly in the long-form benchmark construction and hierarchical evaluation composition, which is useful but not transformative.

The ethics statement is present but relatively high-level. Since the source videos are scraped from YouTube, the paper should more concretely address copyright/licensing, redistribution policy, consent/privacy filtering, and whether videos or only derived prompts/metadata will be released.
